Module 01 · The market

The agent inflection

In twelve months the buyer's question changed from “can it chat?” to “did the work get done?” The numbers below are the ones that survived the hype cycle — and the ones that explain why your finance team is suddenly awake.

01
4 lessons60-sec video5-question quizUpdated 12 Nov 2026

Lesson 01 · The agent inflection00:58

1.1 The number that reframes the year

Menlo Ventures' 2026: The State of Enterprise AI, published 3 November, puts enterprise AI deployment spend at $176.8B by September 2026 — up from $33B a year earlier, a 5.4× increase that is still accelerating (it was 3.9× the year before). The detail that matters more than the total: agents now account for 80% of all tokens on OpenRouter, roughly seven times human-driven usage, with agent traffic up 37× since it overtook human traffic in February.

Read that again in plain language. The majority consumer of frontier models is no longer a person typing. It is software working on someone's behalf, often in loops, often retrying. Every cost, reliability and security problem in the rest of this course follows from that one fact.

$177BEnterprise AI deployment spend, Sep 2026 (from $33B)
80%Of OpenRouter tokens now consumed by agents
5.4×Year-over-year growth in enterprise spend
69%Of deployment dollars captured by frontier labs

1.2 Adoption is real — and sharply bimodal

McKinsey's State of AI survey (fielded May–June 2026, 1,719 respondents across 97 countries) finds 40% of large organizations scaling AI agents in at least one function, up from 27% a year earlier. Among smaller organizations that figure is flat at 22%. Overall, 88% report regular AI use somewhere, and 44% say AI is scaling across the enterprise.

Anthropic's 2026 State of AI Agents report sharpens the picture: 57% of organizations run agents on multi-step workflows, 16% have reached cross-functional or end-to-end processes, and 12% run agents autonomously on complex tasks with limited human oversight. Only 10% still describe their agents as single-step task bots.

The strategic read: agents are not diffusing evenly. They are concentrating in organizations with the process discipline to define a workflow, the data access to feed it, and the review capacity to catch it. That is a capability gap, not a budget gap — which is good news for an operations leader.

1.3 The money follows verifiable work

Of the $77.3B application market, coding ($34.0B) and enterprise chatbots ($25.0B) take 76%. Within coding, the labs' own agents — Claude Code and Codex — account for $24.0B, about 70% of the category. Why coding first? Menlo's answer is the most useful sentence in the report: these are environments where agents can act, workflows they can learn, and results they can verify.

Support and customer success is the next tier at $2.7B, up 4.3× — smaller in absolute terms but growing faster than most categories, and the closest analogue to the work most CX teams own. The enabling infrastructure tells the same story: code sandboxes went from 11% to 40% adoption, search from 5% to 30%, browser infrastructure from 4% to 14%. Those are the three capabilities that turn a model into something that can act.

“AI spend concentrates where agents work best: coding and chatbots make up 76% of the $77.3B app market because they offer environments in which agents can act, workflows they can learn, and results they can verify.”

Menlo Ventures, 2026: The State of Enterprise AI, 3 Nov 2026

1.4 The budget shock nobody planned for

Reported spend averaged 4.7× last year's level against a planned 1.9× — roughly 2.5× plan. The median gap is narrower but still real: 2.2× actual versus 1.8× planned. This is the single most predictable failure mode in an agent program, and it is not a pricing problem. It is an architecture problem: agents re-read context, retry, loop, and call tools in parallel. A workflow that looks like one query in the demo is forty model calls in production.

Module 4 gives you the four levers that control this — caching, routing, step budgets, and model tiering — plus the cheapest new tool of the year, decision models. For now, the takeaway is governance: budget agents by workflow, not by seat, and put a hard step cap on anything that runs unattended.

1.5 Three questions that separate a program from a demo

Every source in this course converges on the same three tests. Ask them early; the answers are cheap and the silence is informative.

1. Can I see the traces? Not the happy-path recording — the full step-by-step log of a real run, including the failures. If the vendor cannot produce one, they have not operated this in production.

2. What is the eval? Which failure modes are measured, on how many examples, and who labels them. “We benchmarked it” is not an answer; benchmarks measure models, evals measure your workflow.

3. What is the blast radius? What can it touch, what can it send, and what happens when it is wrong at 3am. If the answer is “it's very accurate”, you have found the gap.

Agentic AI
Systems that plan and take multi-step actions through tools toward a goal, rather than answering a single prompt.
Deployment spend
Money spent running AI in production, as distinct from model R&D. Menlo's $177B figure is this, not capex.
Token share
The proportion of model input/output processed by agents versus humans. The clearest available proxy for how much work is delegated.
Verifiable output
A result a machine or reviewer can check cheaply — a test that passes, a ticket that closes, a citation that resolves. The strongest predictor of agent ROI.

Module 02 · The machine

Anatomy of an agent

An agent is not a model with a personality. It is a loop with a budget. Getting this picture right is what lets you read a vendor demo without being fooled by it — and debug your own build without guessing.

02
4 lessons60-sec video5-question quizFramework + judgment

Lesson 02 · Anatomy of an agent01:02

2.1 Four parts, one loop

Strip away the branding and every production agent is the same four components: a model that reasons, a harness that runs the control loop, tools that let it act on systems, and context that tells it what is true right now. The loop is unglamorous: assemble context → ask the model for the next action → execute the tool → append the observation → repeat until a stop condition fires.

Two properties of that loop explain most of what you will observe in the field. First, errors compound: at 95% reliability per step, a twenty-step workflow succeeds about 36% of the time. Second, cost compounds too: every iteration re-sends a context window that grows as the run proceeds. Everything else in this course — evals, caching, guardrails — is an answer to one of those two facts.

“The model is the engine. The harness is the car. When you evaluate an agent vendor, you are mostly evaluating their harness — and whether they will show you the traces.”

Course thesis, Module 02

2.2 What the harness actually does

The harness is the part you are really buying, and it is where the engineering lives. A serious harness owns six decisions:

Termination. When does the loop stop — a final answer, a step cap, a wall-clock budget, a confidence floor? An agent without a step cap is an invoice generator.

Context assembly. What enters the window on each turn: system instructions, retrieved documents, tool schemas, prior observations, and a summarised memory of earlier turns.

Tool selection and argument validation. Which tools are visible, how their schemas are described, and what happens when the model calls one with malformed arguments.

Error handling. Retry, repair, escalate to a human, or fail closed. The default in most naive builds is “retry until the budget dies”.

State and durability. Whether a run survives a process restart mid-workflow — the difference between a demo and something you can put behind a queue.

Observability. The trace: every prompt, tool call, observation, token count, and latency. This is the artefact you should demand in any evaluation.

2.3 Context is the product

The 2025–26 craft that replaced “prompt engineering” is context engineering: deciding what the model sees, in what order, at what cost. Four moves carry most of the value. Retrieval puts the right documents in front of the model instead of hoping it remembers. Compaction summarises old turns so a long run doesn't drown in its own history. Structured memory persists facts across sessions — what the customer already told you, which ticket this belongs to. Instruction files — AGENTS.md, agent skills — package the rules of your environment so they don't have to be re-derived every run.

For a CX leader the practical translation is blunt: an agent is only as good as the context you can assemble about a customer at the moment of action. Order history, entitlement, prior contacts, current sentiment, policy version. If that assembly is slow or ambiguous, no model upgrade will save the workflow.

2.4 The four ways agents fail

Practitioners converge on a short list, and it is worth memorising because it maps directly onto what to instrument. It didn't know — missing or stale context, so the model reasoned correctly from false premises. The tool lied — an API returned success with wrong data, or a schema described something the system doesn't do. The loop never ended — no stop condition, or a stop condition the model can talk itself out of. Nobody checked — the output was plausible, unverified, and shipped.

Note that only the first is a model-capability problem. The other three are engineering and process problems you can fix without waiting for a better model — which is exactly why the reliability discipline in Module 5 pays off faster than switching vendors.

2.5 Reading a demo in five minutes

When someone shows you an agent, watch for four tells. Where does the data come from? A demo on curated fixtures will not survive your CRM. What happens on the unhappy path? Ask them to break it — a mistyped order number, an empty record, a permission error. How long did that run take, and what did it cost? If they can't answer, the economics are unmeasured. Can you pause it? Human-in-the-loop is a product feature, not an admission of weakness.

A good vendor answers all four in under five minutes and shows you a trace. A bad one changes the subject to benchmarks.

Harness
The runtime around a model: loop control, tool dispatch, context assembly, state, retries, logging.
Context window
The bounded working memory of a single model call — instructions, retrieved content, tool output, prior turns.
Step budget
A hard cap on loop iterations or spend per run. The cheapest reliability control available.
Trace
The recorded sequence of a run: prompts, tool calls, observations, tokens, latency. The unit of debugging and evaluation.
Compaction
Summarising earlier turns so long runs stay inside the context window at manageable cost.

Q1Which component most determines whether two products using the same model behave differently?

C. Same engine, different car. Termination, context assembly, tool schemas and error handling are the differentiators.

Q2At 95% reliability per step, roughly what is the success rate of a 20-step workflow?

B. 0.95²⁰ ≈ 0.36. Reliability compounds down as step count rises — the core argument for shorter, verifiable workflows.

Q3Which failure class is not primarily a model-capability problem?

B (and C). Tool integrity and verification are engineering and process failures — fixable without a better model. A and D are capability limits.

Q4What does “context engineering” mostly consist of?

A. Retrieval, compaction, structured memory and instruction files — the four moves that carry most of the value.

Q5In a vendor demo, which answer should worry you most?

C. Benchmarks measure models on someone else's tasks. Traces, budgets and pause controls measure your workflow.

Module 03 · The plumbing

The interop stack

For two years every agent integration was bespoke. In 2026 a small set of open standards took over the connective tissue — and moved tool integration from differentiator to commodity. Here is the map, and what it changes about buying.

03
4 lessons60-sec video5-question quizStandards as of Oct 2026

Lesson 03 · The interop stack00:59

3.1 The M×N problem, solved badly for two years

Before standards, connecting an agent to M tools across N agent frameworks meant M×N custom integrations. Every vendor shipped its own connector library, every buyer paid for the same Salesforce integration three times, and nothing was portable. The standards that emerged are not elegant for their own sake — they are an attempt to turn that matrix into two layers: one for tools, one for agents talking to agents.

This matters to a CX leader for a mundane reason. Integration work is where agent budgets quietly die. If your vendor's value proposition is “we already built the connectors”, that value is collapsing — and you should be pricing accordingly.

3.2 The five that matter

MCP — Model Context Protocol. The agent-to-tool and agent-to-data standard. Created by Anthropic in November 2024, now governed by the Agentic AI Foundation under the Linux Foundation, with a current specification revision dated 28 July 2026. One server works across every MCP-capable client, which is why it became the default almost everywhere.

A2A — Agent-to-Agent. Google-originated, now also under neutral Linux Foundation governance. Where MCP connects an agent to a capability, A2A lets one agent delegate to another — including agents you don't operate, across organisational boundaries.

Agent Skills. Packaged procedures an agent loads on demand: a folder of instructions plus scripts and assets, invoked when the task matches. This is how teams ship domain know-how without retraining a model or writing a bespoke tool.

AGENTS.md. A convention rather than a protocol: a file in a repository that tells a coding agent how the project works — build commands, conventions, traps. Trivial, and the highest-leverage adoption in the stack for engineering teams.

AG-UI. The agent-to-frontend layer: a standard event stream so a UI can render what an agent is doing — steps, tool calls, pending approvals — without a bespoke integration per product.

Around the edges sit the commerce protocols — AP2, ACP, UCP — which let an agent transact, and WebMCP, which makes ordinary websites callable by agents. Treat those as directionally important and still settling.

28 JulCurrent MCP spec revision (2026)
5Standards carrying most agent interop today
LFLinux Foundation governance for MCP and A2A
1Server, every client — the MCP promise

3.3 What changed for buyers

Three practical shifts. Portability became real. An MCP server you build or buy keeps working when you change agent framework, model vendor, or interface — so “our connectors are our moat” is no longer a credible lock-in story. Procurement got a checklist. Ask which standards a vendor supports, at which versions, and whether their server is self-hostable. Security moved into the connector. An MCP server is a permission grant with a schema attached; the interesting question is not “does it connect?” but “what can it reach?”

The honest caveat: standards reduce integration cost, they do not reduce integration risk. A standardized connection to your billing system is still a connection to your billing system.

3.4 Where fragmentation still bites

Four seams remain open, and they are where implementations fail in practice. Identity and authorisation — who the agent is acting as, and on whose behalf, is inconsistently modelled across servers. Discovery — finding the right server or agent from thousands, with trustworthy metadata, is unsolved. Semantics — two servers can expose “create ticket” with subtly different behaviour and no way to tell. Audit — a standard trace format across MCP and A2A hops does not really exist yet, so cross-boundary accountability is still hand-built.

And one security note carried into Module 6: MCP's flexibility is also its attack surface. Tool descriptions are text an agent trusts, tool output is content an agent trusts, and both arrive from third parties. Tool poisoning and over-broad scopes are the two failure modes to design against.

“Tool integration is now a commodity. Your differentiation is the workflow, the data, and the guardrails — not the connector.”

Course thesis, Module 03 — see AgentAtlas standards tracker (reviewed Oct 2026)
MCP
Model Context Protocol. Standard connector between an agent and tools/data. Spec revision 2026-07-28.
A2A
Agent-to-Agent. Delegation between agents, including across organisational boundaries.
Agent Skills
Loadable packages of procedure (instructions, scripts, assets) an agent invokes when relevant.
AGENTS.md
Repository-level instruction file read by coding agents. A convention, not a wire protocol.
AG-UI
Standard event stream between an agent and a user interface, for rendering steps and approvals.

Module 04 · Economics

Models, cost, latency

Frontier capability is no longer scarce — it is just expensive. The teams that win in 2026 are the ones that stopped asking “which model is best?” and started asking “which model for this step, at what budget?”

04
4 lessons60-sec video5-question quizPricing as of Nov 2026

Lesson 04 · Models, cost, latency01:01

4.1 A three-horse race with a six-month memory

The frontier has consolidated into three families: Anthropic's Claude, OpenAI's GPT, and Google's Gemini. The cadence that matters is the interval between their releases — GPT-5 in August 2025, Gemini 3 Pro on 18 November 2025, Claude Opus 4.5 on 24 November 2025 — and the fact that the lead has changed hands repeatedly since. Any architecture that assumes one vendor stays best is a bet on a six-month window.

The market data confirms the concentration: frontier labs capture 69% of deployment dollars (up from 50%), and among enterprise API spend Anthropic holds 55% (from 40%), OpenAI 31% (from 27%), with Google falling from 21% to 9%. That is a two-horse race at the top — which is precisely why you should keep a second vendor warm rather than re-platform in a crisis.

4.2 The quiet 2026 innovation: decision models

The most useful new primitive of the year is small and unglamorous. A decision model answers exactly three kinds of question — yes/no, multiple-choice, and rubric scoring — and returns a calibrated probability. Simon Willison tested Google's Gemini Decision 1 against video on 11 November 2026, noting it joins Jev and OpenAI's decision model in the category, priced at 10 cents per million input tokens with output free (Jev being cheapest at 4.2 cents).

Why this matters operationally: the expensive part of an agent is not the final answer, it is the fifty judgement calls on the way there — is this the right ticket, did the tool actually succeed, is this summary faithful, should we escalate. Those are decision-model questions. Routing them to a cheap classifier instead of a frontier model is often a 100× cost reduction on the step that dominates volume.

4.3 Four levers that actually move the bill

Caching. Agents re-read the same system prompt, tool schemas and documents on every step. Prompt and context caching turns a repeated cost into a near-free one, and it is the single highest-leverage optimisation in most deployments.

Routing. Send easy steps to a small model and hard steps to a frontier one. A router plus an escalation rule usually beats a single large model on both cost and latency — provided you can tell which steps were easy, which is an eval problem (Module 5) before it is a routing problem.

Step budgets. A hard cap on iterations per run, with a graceful failure path. This is the only control that bounds a runaway loop, and it should be a product requirement, not an engineering nicety.

Batch and defer. Anything that doesn't need an answer in seconds — nightly summarisation, backfill enrichment, QA sampling — should run asynchronously at a lower price tier.

69%Deployment dollars captured by frontier labs
55 / 31%Anthropic / OpenAI share of enterprise API spend
4.7×Reported spend vs 1.9× planned
$0.10Per million input tokens, Gemini Decision 1

4.4 Latency is a product decision

Users tolerate a slow answer; they do not tolerate an unresponsive interface. Three patterns close most of the gap. Stream the reasoning surface — show the steps as they happen (AG-UI exists for this), so a 40-second run feels like progress rather than a hang. Parallelise independent tool calls; most harnesses serialise by default and leave 2–3× on the table. Speculate on the happy path — pre-fetch the record you are 80% sure is needed, and discard it if not.

Then measure the right number. Mean latency is a vanity metric for agents; p95 time-to-first-useful-token and p99 completion are what your customers experience. Add cost-per-completed-task, not cost-per-token, to the same dashboard.

“A loop that takes forty steps costs forty times a loop that takes one. The bill is an architecture diagram.”

Course thesis, Module 04 — see Willison on decision models, 11 Nov 2026
Decision model
A cheap classifier answering yes/no, choice, or rubric questions with a probability. Used for gates, not generation.
Routing
Choosing a model tier per step based on difficulty, cost, or risk.
Cost per completed task
Total model and tool spend divided by successfully finished work. The only cost metric that survives contact with a P&L.
Open-weight
Models you can host and modify. Rising in usage share, still small in enterprise spend.

Module 05 · Reliability

Reliability and evals

You cannot debug an agent by reading its output. This module is the discipline that separates teams shipping agents from teams demoing them — and it is now a published, teachable craft rather than folklore.

05
4 lessons60-sec video5-question quizMethod + sources

Lesson 05 · Reliability and evals01:02

5.1 Why output review fails

A plausible output can be produced by a broken run. The agent picked the wrong record, the tool returned stale data, it retried four times and landed on the right answer by luck. Reviewing the final artefact tells you nothing about which of those happened — so you cannot tell whether the next run will work. The unit of debugging is the trace, not the output.

This is also the reason “it works in the demo” is not evidence. Demos are curated traces. Production is the distribution.

5.2 Error analysis: the first eval you should run

The method practitioners converged on is borrowed from qualitative research, and it is deliberately low-tech. Collect about thirty real traces from production or realistic staging. Read them one at a time and write, in plain language, what went wrong — no taxonomy yet. This is open coding. As notes accumulate, group the repeated failures into named categories: axial coding. Stop when new traces stop producing new categories — saturation, usually somewhere between twenty and forty traces for a narrow workflow.

The output is a ranked list of failure modes with frequency. That list is your eval specification, your roadmap, and your vendor negotiation document, all at once. Hamel Husain and Shreya Shankar's Evals for AI Engineers (O'Reilly, October 2026) is the current field manual for this; their free Q&A guide covers the same ground. The rule of thumb from Module 2 holds: if you cannot name your top three failure modes, you do not have an agent — you have a demo.

“Read traces and count what breaks before writing an eval. Open coding, axial coding and saturation decide which assertions and binary judges to build.”

AgentEngineering.org, Error Analysis: The First Eval You Should Run, 13 Oct 2026

5.3 Binary assertions beat opinion scores

Once you know the failure modes, encode each as a binary assertion — a check that returns pass or fail with a reason. Did the agent cite a source that exists? Did it call the correct tool? Did it stop before the step cap? Did the refund amount match policy? Binary checks are consistent, cheap to re-run, and easy to argue about with stakeholders, which is a feature.

Where judgement is unavoidable, use a model as a judge — carefully. Publish the rubric, force a binary or small ordinal output, randomise option order to counter position bias, and spot-check the judge against human labels on a sample. A judge you have not calibrated is an opinion with a compute bill. One-to-ten scores feel informative and are usually noise; a pass/fail with a written reason is worth more.

5.4 The four-layer eval stack

Tool evals. Does each tool return correct data under realistic failures — timeouts, empty results, permission errors? Cheap, fast, and catches a surprising share of production incidents.

Trajectory evals. Did the agent take a sane path: right tools, sensible order, no wasteful loops? This is where step-level efficiency and cost live.

End-to-end evals. Did the task succeed, judged against a task-specific check or a calibrated judge, on a regression set that grows every time you find a new failure.

Online monitors. Live signals on production traffic: escalation rate, tool-error rate, retry depth, cost per task, human override rate. Evals tell you what you fixed; monitors tell you what you broke.

5.5 Designing the human in the loop

Human review is a scarce resource and should be spent where mistakes are expensive and irreversible. Three patterns work. Approve-before-act for anything that leaves the building: refunds, outbound email, contract terms. Sample-and-audit for high-volume low-risk work — review 2–5% with a structured rubric, and track the disagreement rate. Escalate-on-uncertainty: let the agent hand off with its context attached, so the human starts informed rather than from scratch.

The failure mode to avoid is review theatre — a queue nobody reads, which converts a safety control into a liability. If a review step has no measured effect on outcomes, delete it and put the effort into an assertion instead.

Error analysis
Reading real traces, naming failures in plain language, and grouping them until categories saturate.
Binary assertion
A pass/fail check encoding a known failure mode. The workhorse of agent evals.
Trajectory eval
Judging the path taken — tools, order, loop depth — rather than only the final output.
Regression set
A growing collection of cases that must keep passing. Every new failure becomes a fixture.
Judge calibration
Agreement testing between a model judge and human labels on a sample, before trusting it.

Module 06 · Trust & rollout

Security, governance, and the 90-day plan

An agent with the wrong three permissions is a data exfiltration tool with a friendly interface. This module gives you the threat model that survived the year, the controls that actually work, and a deployment plan you can defend in a steering meeting.

06
4 lessons60-sec video5-question quizThreat model + plan

Lesson 06 · Security and the 90 days01:01

6.1 The lethal trifecta

Simon Willison's framing from June 2025 is still the clearest threat model in the field, and 2026 gave it more evidence rather than less. The three legs are: access to private data, exposure to untrusted content, and the ability to communicate externally. An agent with all three can be induced to send your data out, because instructions hidden in a document, a web page, a ticket or an email are indistinguishable from the user's own instructions at the model level.

The uncomfortable part: no prompt reliably fixes this. Prompt injection is not a bug being patched; it is a structural property of systems that read instructions and data through the same channel. Any vendor claiming “we've solved prompt injection” is telling you they have not modelled it.

“Any time you grant an LLM-based system access to private data, exposure to untrusted content, and the ability to externally communicate, you have a nasty security hole.”

Simon Willison, lethal-trifecta tag — framing from June 2025, still current Nov 2026

6.2 Six patterns that defuse it

The design principle is simple: don't ask the model to resist — make the attack structurally impossible. Remove a leg, and the exfiltration path disappears.

1. Cut the data leg. Scope retrieval to what this task needs, at the row and field level, not the whole knowledge base. Prefer read-only projections over raw records.

2. Cut the egress leg. Allowlist outbound destinations. A tool that can “send” to an arbitrary address is an exfiltration primitive; one that can only file into your ticketing system is not.

3. Quarantine untrusted content. Fetch and summarise untrusted material in a separate call with no tools attached, then pass only the summary into the acting loop.

4. Capability-scope every tool. Least privilege, per task, with expiry. An agent handling a refund query does not need account-deletion rights.

5. Human-gate irreversible actions. Anything that spends money, changes a contract, deletes data or leaves the building gets an approval step — with the proposed action shown, not just a summary.

6. Sandbox execution. Code and browser tools run in an isolated environment with an explicit network policy, because tool output is attacker-controlled by definition.

6.3 Governance that isn't paperwork

Six artefacts, each with an operational purpose. An agent inventory — what exists, what it can reach, who owns it. Most organisations cannot produce this list, which is the finding. A named owner per agent, on the business side, not just engineering. A data classification map so permissions can be derived rather than negotiated. A permission matrix reviewed on a schedule, because scopes accumulate silently. Retained audit logs — every tool call, every approval, every override, for a defined period. A kill switch and an incident runbook that someone has actually rehearsed.

Then add the commercial control: a standards and audit clause in every agent contract — which protocols, which trace format, export rights on termination. Portability is a governance property as much as a technical one.

6.4 The 30 / 60 / 90

Days 1–30: pick one workflow and prove the economics. Criteria: verifiable output, a named business owner, high volume, contained blast radius, and an existing baseline you can measure against. Write the eval set from thirty traces. Do not scale in this phase, and do not let a second workflow in.

Days 31–60: build the instrumentation. Trace logging, the four-layer eval stack, a cost-per-completed-task dashboard, the permission matrix, and one rehearsed failure drill. Budget the step cap and the spend cap in the same document.

Days 61–90: expand only where the numbers hold. Add the second workflow only if the first hit its quality bar and its cost target. Publish a one-page scorecard to your leadership: tasks completed, escalation rate, cost per task, incidents. Expansion without that scorecard is how the 4.7× budget surprise happens.

6.5 What to watch in the next two quarters

Agent identity. Delegated authority — an agent acting on behalf of a specific human, with that scope auditable — is the missing primitive, and the standards bodies know it.

Cross-boundary audit. A trace format that survives MCP and A2A hops. Until it exists, multi-vendor agent chains are hard to hold accountable.

Commerce protocols. AP2, ACP and UCP will decide whether “agent buys things” becomes a mainstream workflow or stays a pilot.

Decision models as default gates. Cheap classifiers inside every loop, which quietly changes what a “quality check” costs.

Open-weight economics. Usage share is rising faster than spend; the moment a credible open-weight agent stack undercuts frontier pricing on a common workflow, the routing calculus in Module 4 changes.

Lethal trifecta
Private data + untrusted content + external communication. All three together enables exfiltration.
Prompt injection
Instructions hidden in content the agent reads, treated as if the user issued them. Structural, not a patchable bug.
Egress allowlist
An explicit list of destinations an agent may send to. Removes the third leg of the trifecta.
Blast radius
Everything an agent can touch, send or destroy if it behaves badly. The first thing to bound.
Kill switch
A rehearsed, one-step way to halt all agent actions. Tested, not merely documented.

Module 06 — check your read

5 questions

Q1Which combination defines the lethal trifecta?

C. Remove any one leg and the exfiltration path disappears.

Q2What is the correct response to prompt injection risk?

A. Instructions and data share a channel. Prompts reduce frequency; architecture removes consequence.

Q3Which control most directly removes the egress leg?

D. If the agent can only file into your ticketing system, it cannot exfiltrate to an attacker's address.

Q4What belongs in the first 30 days of an agent rollout?

B. Prove the economics on one bounded workflow before touching a second.

Q5Which governance artefact do most organisations fail to produce, and is therefore the usual finding?

C. You cannot govern, scope or kill what you cannot enumerate — and scopes accumulate silently.

The vendor question sheet

Ask thisWhat a good answer sounds like
Show me a trace of a failed production run.A real step-by-step log with tool calls, latencies and token counts — not a screen recording.
What are your top three failure modes, and how are they measured?Named modes, binary assertions, a regression set that grows.
Which standards, at which versions, and can we self-host the connector?MCP revision, A2A support, AG-UI event stream, export rights.
What is the step cap, and what happens when it's hit?A hard limit with a graceful handoff to a human, configured by you.
What can the agent reach and send?Scoped permissions, egress allowlist, per-task capability grants with expiry.
What is cost per completed task, including retries?A measured number from their own deployment, with the denominator defined.
Where does the human approve?Specific actions listed — money, outbound comms, data deletion, contract terms.
What is the exit?Data export on termination, no proprietary trace format, documented model portability.

Glossary

Agent
Model + harness + tools + context, running a loop until a stop condition.
Harness
The runtime: loop control, tool dispatch, context assembly, state, retries, tracing.
Context engineering
Deciding what the model sees, in what order, at what cost — retrieval, compaction, memory, instruction files.
MCP / A2A
Standard for agent↔tool/data (MCP) and agent↔agent (A2A) connections.
Decision model
Cheap classifier for yes/no, choice or rubric questions — the quality gate that costs cents.
Trace
The recorded run: prompts, tool calls, observations, tokens, latency. Unit of debugging.
Binary assertion
Pass/fail check encoding a known failure mode. More reliable than 1–10 scoring.
Lethal trifecta
Private data + untrusted content + external communication. All three = exfiltration risk.
Blast radius
Everything the agent can touch, send or destroy if it misbehaves.
Cost per completed task
Total spend ÷ successfully finished work. The only agent cost metric a CFO accepts.
